A sequence, top to bottom. Three columns: Git, the helper, the server.
slides.text:
Git                              credential helper                 server (GitHub)
    |                                                                    |
    |------------------- request without a credential ------------------>|
    |<------------------ 401: authentication required -------------------|
    |                                                                    |
    |-- get (protocol, host) ----------->|                               |
    |<-- username, password (a token) ---|      (none stored: Git prompts, or fails where
    |                                    |       prompts are disabled)   |
    |------------------- request with the credential ------------------->|
    |                                                                    |
    |   200  -> store  ------------------>|   kept for next time         |
    |   401  -> erase  ------------------>|   removed; Git asks again next time
    |   403 / 404 -> (nothing)            |   the helper's store is unchanged

slides.lead: You should now be able to say:
items: Authentication is which account; authorization is what that account may do; the error text can be the same for both.
Over HTTPS the secret is a token, and Git obtains it from a list of credential helpers, asked in order.
Git calls get before a request, store after success and erase after a 401; after a 403 or 404 it changes nothing.
GIT_TRACE=1 shows which helper ran; gh auth status shows which account.
A helper can be scoped to a host, a username or a path, and an empty value resets the list.

beats.text: You gave Ravi write access to the work repository on Monday. On Wednesday his push, the upload of his commits, still fails with 403, and Git never asks him for anything. No prompt, no chance to type a different credential. Your CTO asks: why?
beats.tele: You gave Ravi write access to the work repository on Monday. On Wednesday his push, the upload of his commits, still fails with 403, and Git never asks him for anything. No prompt, no chance to type a different credential. Your CTO asks: why?

beats.text: Because his keychain, the Mac's password store, holds a credential for another account. A 403 doesn't make Git discard it, so Git keeps sending it. Granting access to his work account changed nothing, because that account never arrives at the server.
beats.tele: Because his keychain, the Mac's password store, holds a credential for another account. A 403 doesn't make Git discard it, so Git keeps sending it. Granting access to his work account changed nothing, because that account never arrives at the server.

beats.text: Which transport and which server? That's decided by the remote URL, after rewrites, and the evidence is git remote -v. Which credential does the client present? Decided by Git's credential helpers for HTTPS, and by ssh, its configuration and the agent for SSH. And: who does the server say you are, and what may that identity do? Decided by GitHub.

beats.text: Git has no accounts and no passwords. It delegates the connection to a transport. Over HTTPS, Git speaks HTTP and attaches a username and a secret obtained from a credential helper or a prompt. For GitHub the secret is a token, a string that stands for an account with a subset of its rights. Over SSH, Git starts the ssh program, which proves possession of a private key. Git never sees the key.
beats.tele: Git has no accounts and no passwords. It delegates the connection to a transport. Over HTTPS, Git speaks HTTP and attaches a username and a secret obtained from a credential helper or a prompt. For GitHub the secret is a token, a string that stands for an account with a subset of its rights. Over SSH, Git starts the `ssh` program, which proves possession of a private key. Git never sees the key.

beats.text: The server maps the token or key to an account, which is authentication. Then it evaluates roles, token permissions and organization rules for the repository, which is authorization.
beats.tele: The server maps the token or key to an account, which is authentication. Then it evaluates roles, token permissions and organization rules for the repository, which is authorization.

beats.text: Three identities are involved in everyday work, and they're independent. The commit identity: the author and committer name and email written into commits, set by user.name and user.email, checked by nobody. It's an assertion. The authentication identity: the GitHub account that a token or SSH key belongs to, checked by GitHub on every connection.
beats.tele: Three identities are involved in everyday work, and they're independent. The commit identity: the author and committer name and email written into commits, set by `user.name` and `user.email`, checked by nobody. It's an assertion. The authentication identity: the GitHub account that a token or SSH key belongs to, checked by GitHub on every connection.

beats.text: The signing identity: the key that signed a commit or tag. You can push commits written by anyone, as any account that has Write, signed by any key or none. "It says Asha in the log" is not evidence of who pushed.
beats.tele: The signing identity: the key that signed a commit or tag. You can push commits written by anyone, as any account that has Write, signed by any key or none. "It says Asha in the log" is not evidence of who pushed.

beats.text: HTTPS. In one sentence: over HTTPS, GitHub accepts a token in the place where HTTP expects a password, and nothing else. GitHub has not accepted account passwords for Git since the thirteenth of August 2021. Git still calls the secret a password, because to Git it is one: the prompt reads "Password for", and you'll see it. In practice nobody should type a token: the GitHub CLI or Git Credential Manager obtains one through the browser and hands it to Git.

beats.text: Now the protocol. In one sentence: when a server demands authentication, Git asks each configured credential helper in turn, then falls back to prompting, and afterwards tells the helpers whether the credential worked.
beats.tele: Now the protocol. In one sentence: when a server demands authentication, Git asks each configured credential helper in turn, then falls back to prompting, and afterwards tells the helpers whether the credential worked.

beats.text: A helper is a program that Git runs with one argument, get, store or erase, and a description of the request on standard input as key=value lines: protocol, host, and optionally path and username. git credential fill, approve and reject drive the same machinery by hand, so the whole exchange can be watched without a server.
beats.tele: A helper is a program that Git runs with one argument, `get`, `store` or `erase`, and a description of the request on standard input as `key=value` lines: `protocol`, `host`, and optionally `path` and `username`. `git credential fill`, `approve` and `reject` drive the same machinery by hand, so the whole exchange can be watched without a server.

beats.text: Quick quiz, before the table. Git sends a stored credential, and the server answers 403. What does Git tell the helper: store, erase, or nothing? Say it out loud.
beats.tele: Quick quiz, before the table. Git sends a stored credential, and the server answers 403. What does Git tell the helper: store, erase, or nothing? Say it out loud.

beats.text: A request needs a credential: the helper's store is read, get. The server accepted it: the store is written, store. The server answered 401: the entry is removed, erase. The server answered 403 or 404: the store is unchanged. So the quiz answer is nothing. If you said erase, you expected Git to tidy up, and that's a reasonable thing to expect.
beats.tele: A request needs a credential: the helper's store is read, `get`. The server accepted it: the store is written, `store`. The server answered 401: the entry is removed, `erase`. The server answered 403 or 404: the store is unchanged. So the quiz answer is nothing. If you said erase, you expected Git to tidy up, and that's a reasonable thing to expect.

beats.text: That last row is from Git's source: the reject is called for a 401 with a credential that was sent, and for nothing else on this path. In all four rows the working tree, the index, HEAD, the refs and the Git configuration are unchanged.

beats.text: Which helper answers? credential.helper is a list. Git asks each helper in order and stops at the first that returns a username and a password. An empty value resets the list, which is how a later configuration file discards helpers set by an earlier one. credential.<URL>.helper and credential.<URL>.username apply only to matching URLs, and credential.useHttpPath makes the repository path part of the lookup. By default a credential is per host, not per repository.

beats.text: osxkeychain ships with Git on macOS and keeps the secret in the login keychain. It stores whatever you typed. The GitHub CLI configures itself as a helper for https://github.com, and keeps its token in the system credential store, or in a plain text file if none is available.

beats.text: Git Credential Manager, value manager, obtains tokens through the browser and is installed separately. store writes a plain text file. The manual calls it discouraged, so don't use it. cache keeps the secret in the memory of a background process and isn't used in this course, because it starts a daemon.

beats.text: Inside .git: nothing. A credential is never stored in the repository unless you put it there. The helper list is configuration, usually at system or global scope.

beats.text: And that explains a rule of this course: labs/shell and the replays switch off the system configuration, where macOS installations of Git usually configure osxkeychain. That's why the labs that contact GitHub run in your normal shell. In the lab, Git finds no helper. In your normal shell, it finds whichever one is configured.

beats.text: Two analogies from the textbook.
beats.tele: Two analogies from the textbook.

beats.text: For the distinction: a badge reader and a door list. The reader checks that the badge is real and whose it is. The list on each door says which badge holders may enter. The analogy breaks because GitHub often gives the same answer to both failures: an unknown badge and a known badge without access can both get "there is no such door". The error text alone doesn't tell you which check failed.

The error text alone doesn't tell you which check failed.

beats.text: For the protocol: a receptionist with a key cabinet. Asked for a key, the receptionist looks in the cabinet: get. If the visitor had to bring their own key and it opened the door, it's hung in the cabinet: store. If a key from the cabinet didn't open the door, it's thrown away: erase. The analogy breaks at the last step: the receptionist throws a key away only when the door says "wrong key", 401, not when it says "you may not enter", 403.

beats.text: Git sends a request, and the server demands authentication. Git asks the helper: get, with the protocol and the host. The helper answers with a username and a password, which for GitHub is a token. Git repeats the request with it.
beats.tele: Git sends a request, and the server demands authentication. Git asks the helper: `get`, with the protocol and the host. The helper answers with a username and a password, which for GitHub is a token. Git repeats the request with it.

beats.text: Then three outcomes. Accepted: Git tells the helper store. A 401, wrong credential: Git tells the helper erase, and next time it will ask again. A 403 or a 404: Git tells the helper nothing. The wrong account stays in the cabinet and answers every later request.

beats.text: An empty value resets the list for that host, and what follows it replaces every helper configured before. Now github.com gets the work account and another host still gets the personal one.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. Ravi's Wednesday, worked through the three questions. Transport and server: git remote -v shows an HTTPS URL on github.com. Fine. Which credential does the client present? GIT_TRACE=1 on a dry-run push names the helper, and gh auth status names the account. It's his personal account: he once cloned a personal project over HTTPS, and the keychain stored it. Who does the server say he is? A valid account without permission: 403.
